newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German IBIS DAX index scores record close.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German IBIS DAX index scores record close.

text.p: Germany's DAX index ended bourse trade at a record closing high on Wednesday and shares continued their strong run into afternoon electronic business, supported by the sturdy dollar and a firm Wall Street opening.
The DAX index finished bourse dealings at a record close of 3,364.99, up 44.33 points or 1.33 percent.
The IBIS DAX ended electronic trade at 3,375.45, up 30.36 points or 0.91 percent. This was off an all-time high of 3,392.13 hit earlier but still at a record closing level.
The peak of 3,392.13 was not far from the next important market resistance level of 3,400 points.

"There are some decent volumes there and the greenback is is helping, especially with the exporters. The slogan at the moment seems to be -- enjoy it and let the cash roll in," Josh Waiblinger of equity sales at BHF Bank.

Further support came from comments by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, who said that the U.S. stock market might be reasonably priced, provided analysts' forecasts of future earnings prove right.
Last week he had suggested that stock prices might be too high.
"The markets digested his comments and didn't find anything bearish in them," one trader said.
The Dow Jones industrial average on Wall Street was more than half a percent higher as share trade in Frankfurt ended.
Dealers expressed admiration for the market's resilience in the face of fundamental factors which hardly indicated a vigorous economic recovery but did quell most fears of inflation.

The strength of the dollar at 1.71 marks, around 34-month highs and seemingly unstoppable at the moment, was viewed by market operators as a panacea for any wobbles, woes or potential jitters on the German share bourse.

The market shrugged off concern over unspectacular German economic growth after fourth-quarter gross domestic product figures showed only a 0.1 percent rise, up 2.2 percent from the year-earlier quarter.
January industry output figures showed a 1.7 percent drop, mainly driven by a 25 percent month-on-month fall in the construction industry.

Sharp fluctuations in the 30-share DAX barely raise an eyebrow in Frankfurt these days. "100-point shifts have almost become normal. This kind of volatility is definitely not as shocking as it was a couple of years ago," said Waiblinger.
Shares in the limelight included Deutsche Lufthansa AG, which ended up 64 pfennigs at 23.87 marks but off earlier highs.
Traders had identified a large domestic buyer buying huge amounts of the stock, which was lifted by a Boeing report which forecast a 4.4 percent increase in air travel in Europe.
Tyre-maker Continental AG ended the day up 1.12 marks at 34.75 marks after it said its 1996 pre-tax profits were up 68.2 percent at 328 million marks ($192).

Defence and engineering group Rheinmetall AG ended up 9.62 percent at 285 marks after it said it would be seeking to secure a majority stake in car components manufacturer Kolbenschmidt AG this year. ($ = 1.712 German Marks)
